# HawkEye

> HawkEye is a website, API, cron job and DNS monitoring service. It checks your websites and APIs on a schedule, checks a failure again 15 seconds later and opens an incident only when that fails too, notices when a scheduled job stops pinging or reports a failure, notices when a DNS record disappears or changes, and alerts you by email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord, Telegram, PagerDuty or webhook. It also warns you before SSL certificates and domain registrations expire.

HawkEye is for freelancers, web agencies, small businesses and small development teams. There is a free plan (not a trial) and paid plans; the home page shows current prices and limits.

## What it does

- Set up from your domain: enter a domain and HawkEye looks at the site from outside and suggests monitors (the home page, a health endpoint such as /healthz, an api subdomain, the domain's MX records); you pick which to add.
- Website and API monitoring: custom request methods, headers, bodies, Basic/bearer/API-key authentication, and checks of the status code and response content: text the page must or must not contain, and JSON values (equals, contains, exists, and number comparisons such as queue_size at most 500). "Send test request" in the form shows the response once, without storing it, and clicking a field of a JSON response adds a check for it. Optionally, each check sends a W3C traceparent header so it appears in the site's own distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry, Datadog, Honeycomb, Grafana), with the trace ID shown in the check history.
- Cron job (heartbeat) monitoring, on every plan: a job requests its private ping address each time it runs; a late ping, a failure ping or a non-zero exit status opens an incident and alerts you.
- DNS monitoring, on every plan: HawkEye looks up an A, AAAA, MX, NS or TXT record on a schedule and alerts you when it disappears or stops matching the value you expect, and (DNS change alerts, on by default) when it changes at all, showing before and after: a new mail server, name servers that aren't yours, an edited SPF or DMARC record. A changed address isn't alerted while a CDN rotates within the addresses seen in the last 7 days. "Set up from your domain" suggests change monitors for the domain's name servers, mail, SPF and DMARC records.
- Response-time tracking, uptime reports and incident history. Each website and API check is split into DNS lookup, connect, TLS handshake and server wait (time to first byte), shown per check and as an average for any period, so a slowdown can be traced to DNS, the network, the certificate setup or the application.
- Keyword monitoring: alert when a page stops containing a phrase or starts showing one (with one-click checks for common failures such as a WordPress database error or a parked domain).
- Embeddable uptime badges for a website or a GitHub README, opt-in per monitor.
- Import from OpenAPI or Postman: upload or paste an OpenAPI 3.x or Swagger 2.0 file (JSON or YAML) or a Postman collection (v2.x), read in the browser, and HawkEye lists an API check per endpoint, checking the status code (and, from OpenAPI, the response's required fields); health and read endpoints are ticked, writes are listed unticked, credentials are entered once, and the checks are tagged with the API's name. On every plan, within its monitor limit.
- Paste a cURL command: the API check form and each multi-step step can be filled in from a cURL command (including a browser's Copy as cURL), read in the browser; tokens and keys go into the encrypted credentials field.
- Multi-step API checks: several requests in a row, such as signing in and then fetching an account with the returned token, with values passed between steps, encrypted secrets, a test run before saving (showing each step's response with secrets hidden, where clicking a field adds a check or saves the value for later steps), and alerts that name the failing step. Free includes one of up to 3 steps; Pro 5 and Agency 50, of up to 10 steps.
- Re-check before alerting, on every plan: when a healthy monitor fails, HawkEye checks it again from the same location 15 seconds later instead of waiting for the next scheduled check, so a real outage alerts in seconds and a single blip alerts nobody. On by default for requests that are safe to repeat (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and DNS lookups); a monitor that sends POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE is re-checked only if its owner turns it on. Re-checks show in the check history but don't count in uptime.
- Slow-response alerts: an alert when a site stays slower than a threshold you choose for several checks in a row (saying which part of the request got slower compared with the past week), and another when it is back to normal.
- Alerts by email, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Discord or Telegram, PagerDuty (incidents that open on an outage and resolve on recovery), or signed JSON webhook, routed per client by tag, with optional alert delays and quiet hours per monitor.
- Public status pages for your customers: one on the Free plan, several on paid plans (one per client or product), with incident updates you post while you work on a problem. On the Agency plan each page can be served at an address on the client's own domain (such as status.yourclient.com): add a CNAME and a TXT record, and HawkEye verifies them and looks after the certificate.
- Maintenance windows that pause alerts during planned work (paid plans).
- Deploys from CI: two lines in a pipeline quiet alerts for the monitors a deploy affects (by tag, ending by themselves after up to 2 hours; paid plans), then end the quiet period and check those sites at once, failing the pipeline if one is down (the check works on every plan). Uses a "deploys only" API key, safe to store in CI. A GitHub Action (EssenceOfChaos/hawkeye/actions/deploy) and a GitLab CI snippet. Guide: https://hawkeye.observer/docs/deploys
- AI-drafted incident updates (paid plans, off until the owner turns them on): a "Draft with AI" button writes a first draft of a status page update from the incident's details (never the monitor's address or response content) with Claude Haiku 5.5 by Anthropic; nothing is posted until the owner edits and posts it.
- SSL certificate expiry warnings 30, 14, 7 and 1 days before expiry, on every plan.
- Domain registration expiry warnings on the same schedule, for a number of domains that depends on the plan. Some domain registries do not publish expiry dates; HawkEye says so rather than guessing.
- Checks from several locations on paid plans, where offered.
- Works with Claude: HawkEye is listed in Claude's connector directory (https://claude.ai/directory/hawkeye; add it there or in Claude under Customize, then Connectors, and sign in to HawkEye). The MCP server at https://hawkeye.observer/mcp also lets Claude Code and other MCP clients read monitors, uptime and incidents, suggest monitors for a domain, and, with a read and write key, add monitors on every plan and (on paid plans) pause monitors, set up and test multi-step API checks (it names the secrets a check needs; a person enters them in HawkEye), post incident updates and schedule maintenance. It uses the same API keys, or MCP clients can connect by signing in (OAuth with PKCE).
- Claude Code plugin (/plugin marketplace add EssenceOfChaos/hawkeye, then /plugin install hawkeye@hawkeye): sets up monitoring from a repository. It finds the production domain, cron jobs and scheduled tasks, suggests monitors, and after the person approves the plan creates them (a heartbeat per job) and adds the ping to each job, with ping addresses kept in environment variables or CI secrets. Works on every plan with a read and write key. Guide: https://hawkeye.observer/docs/claude#setup
- Codex plugin (codex plugin marketplace add EssenceOfChaos/hawkeye, codex plugin add hawkeye@hawkeye, then codex mcp login hawkeye to sign in to HawkEye): the same monitoring setup from a repository, and the same MCP tools for asking about monitors, uptime and incidents. Signs in through OAuth, so there is no key to copy; an API key in ~/.codex/config.toml also works. Guide: https://hawkeye.observer/docs/codex
- Sign in with Google or GitHub, or with an email address and password: one account can use any of them, and the sign-in page marks the one used last on that browser. Only the account ID and email address are received.
- Two-factor sign-in with an authenticator app, with recovery codes, on every plan; on a team, the owner can require it for everyone (it applies after Google and GitHub too).
- A security log on every plan: the owner sees who changed what in the organization (monitors, status pages, maintenance, incident updates, alert recipients, API keys, connected apps, team), when, from where, and with which API key or connected app; each person sees their own sign-ins, including failed ones. Kept for a year.
- A public API with API keys: read-only or read and write keys on every plan. On Free a read and write key can add monitors (within the plan's limits) and make no other change; on paid plans it can make every change the API offers. Keys expire after 90 days unless the owner chooses otherwise, and can be revoked at any time.

## Pages

- [Home, features and pricing](https://hawkeye.observer/)
- [About HawkEye](https://hawkeye.observer/about): who builds HawkEye and why, its principles (simple, effective, secure) and the technology it runs on (Go, PostgreSQL, React)
- [Sign up](https://hawkeye.observer/register)
- [Multi-step API checks guide](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/api-workflows)
- [HawkEye status](https://status.hawkeye.observer): whether HawkEye itself is up, measured every minute from outside its own servers, with 90 days of uptime and any incidents
- [Free tools](https://hawkeye.observer/tools): [Is My Website Down?](https://hawkeye.observer/tools/is-website-down) (whether a public site answers, its status code and response time), [SSL Certificate Checker](https://hawkeye.observer/tools/ssl-certificate-checker) (certificate expiry, issuer and trust for any public domain), [Uptime SLA Calculator](https://hawkeye.observer/tools/uptime-sla-calculator) (allowed downtime for an uptime percentage) and [Downtime Cost Calculator](https://hawkeye.observer/tools/downtime-cost-calculator) (revenue at risk from an outage)
- [Documentation](https://hawkeye.observer/docs): [Getting started](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/getting-started), [Heartbeat (cron job) monitoring](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/cron-job-monitoring), [DNS monitoring](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/dns-monitoring), [Alerts](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/alerts), [Deploys and CI](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/deploys), [API and API keys](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/api), [Use HawkEye with Claude](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/claude) and [Use HawkEye with Codex](https://hawkeye.observer/docs/codex)
